name: Two-Rook Checkmate
summary: The two-rook or "ladder" mate drives a lone king to the edge with alternating rook checks — the first checkmate every player should learn.
intro: Two rooks deliver checkmate against a lone king with no help at all from their own king. Working as a pair, the rooks cut off successive ranks and march the defending king to the edge of the board, where a final check ends the game. Because the method is so mechanical, it is usually the very first checkmate a beginner learns.
boardCaption: Two rooks versus a lone king: White to play and drive the black king up the board to mate.
line: Rb5+ Kd6 Ra6+ Kd7 Rb7+ Kd8 Ra8#

sections.heading: How the ladder works
paragraphs: The two rooks form a "ladder." One rook checks the king along a rank, forcing it to step back a row; the other rook then checks along the next rank, pushing the king back again. Rung by rung the king is driven to the edge, where the last check is mate.

The only thing to watch for is the defending king walking toward a rook. If the king approaches the rook that is about to give check, simply swing that rook to the far side of the board — its full width keeps it safe — and carry on with the ladder from a distance.

sections.heading: The demonstration
paragraphs: In the diagram the rooks stand ready on the a- and b-files. 1.Rb5+ pushes the king to the sixth rank, 2.Ra6+ drives it to the seventh, and 3.Rb7+ forces it to the eighth. With the king trapped on the back rank, 4.Ra8# completes the ladder: one rook guards the eighth rank while the other covers the seventh, and the king has no escape.
Notice that the white king never moved a single square. Two rooks are enough on their own, which is what makes this mate so fast — often quicker than shepherding an extra pawn to promotion.

sections.heading: Avoiding stalemate
paragraphs: The one real trap is stalemate. If you check with a rook while the enemy king is already on the edge with no legal square, and it is not genuinely in check, the game is an immediate draw. Make sure the king always has somewhere to step — right up until the move that is checkmate.
A safe habit is to keep both rooks active and never give a pointless check. If in doubt, make a quiet waiting move with a rook along the far edge before delivering the final blow.

keyIdeas: Two rooks mate a lone king with no help from their own king.
The rooks alternate checks, each cutting off a rank and pushing the king back one row.
If the king attacks a rook, slide that rook to the far end of the same rank and continue.
Mate arrives with the king on the edge, one rook checking along it and the other guarding the next rank.
Beware stalemate: never give a check that leaves the king with no move unless it is mate.

white: Alternate rook checks to drive the king toward the nearest edge.
When the king nears a rook, shift that rook to the far side and keep the ladder going.
Deliver mate with the king on the edge and both rooks controlling the last two rows.
black: Walk the king toward the rooks to harass them and try to win a tempo.
Watch for stalemate tricks if the stronger side grows careless.
Keep the king as central as possible for as long as possible.
